evidence_set: The authors name as limits that amount used per day could not be compared (the units for e-cigarettes and cigarettes differ, because e-cigarette products vary in device, liquid nicotine concentration and flavour), that duration of use could not be reliably calculated, and that most adults who had used e-cigarettes in the past 30 days also used other products, so dependence is hard to attribute to one product (they were excluded). They call for future studies of exposure biomarkers such as cotinine and of how dependence develops over time and differs by device and liquid characteristics, noting that the longitudinal design of PATH will help. Editors' reading: the dependence items are self-reported; the design is a single survey wave, so nothing follows people over time.

As described by the National Academies: a separate analysis of PATH Wave 1 (437 adults who used only e-cigarettes in the past year, daily or not, and 8,689 who only smoked cigarettes) used a 16-item dependence index tested for equal validity across products. Average severity was 1.37 standard deviation units lower for the e-cigarette-only group than for the cigarette-only group, comparable to cigar-only and higher among daily than non-daily e-cigarette-only participants (difference 0.40 SD). 3 of the 24 items were dropped as invalid indicators and 16 were retained as having minimal or no differential validity across products. The sample partly overlaps Liu et al. (same survey wave; this analysis included daily and non-daily users, Liu et al. daily users); the committee calls the two non-redundant data sources, but the editors count them as one dataset.

As described by the National Academies: a voluntary anonymous web survey (December 2012 to August 2014; 3,609 people who vaped every day and had not smoked in the past 30 days, recruited on vaping and medical websites; 42% reported advocating for e-cigarettes online) compared dependence on e-cigarettes with their recall of earlier smoking: mean index 8.1 (SD 3.5) vs 14.5 (3.7). E-cigarette scores were higher with longer use, larger devices with a button, higher price and a higher nicotine concentration of the liquid. A second analysis of the same data (1,048 first-generation vs 3,373 advanced devices) found higher scores with advanced devices (8.3 vs 7.1 with first-generation) and a shorter time to first use after waking (38.7 vs 67.3 minutes), although their liquid had a lower nicotine concentration (15.1 vs 19.1 mg/mL). The committee notes the sample is not representative and that recall of earlier smoking could bias the comparison.

The UK review states that there was substantial evidence from previous reports (National Academies, the Committee on Toxicity and its own 2018 report) that vaping can result in symptoms of nicotine dependency, and moderate evidence that the risk and severity are lower than for cigarette smoking and vary with product characteristics such as device type and nicotine concentration; its pharmacokinetic review is consistent with this. It adds that many scales are used and there is no consensus on the best scale for vaping dependence, which makes comparison with smoking difficult, and cites a systematic review suggesting higher nicotine concentrations might increase abuse potential and appeal. The grading statements rest on earlier reports and existing evidence, not a new independent finding; the point about scales is this review's own finding.

evidence_set: In 17 adults who vaped daily (9 also smoked), using three tobacco-flavoured products chosen by the researchers and with their own breath before the first puff as the control, the first breath after one puff held nicotine in all but one person (median 108 ng, up to 2,140 ng), propylene glycol in 4 of 17 (up to 127 µg; median below the limit), glycerol in none (below the limit of quantification), tobacco-specific nitrosamines, measured in 9 people (total up to 77 pg as NDMA equivalent, median 28 pg, lowest value below the limit of quantification; no difference between people who also smoked and people who only vaped, p = 0.79), formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein in none of the 4 tested, and of 13 metals in 3 people only copper (up to 2.92 ng). Only the first exhalation after each puff was sampled.

Modelled scenarios, not measurements in any person nearby: a car (2 people vaping at 0.5 puffs a minute for 1 hour in 2 m3 with no ventilation, the bystander a child; the authors say it approximates the highest exposure expected in everyday situations) and an office (1 person at 2 puffs a minute for 4 hours in 30 m3 with ventilation of 0.5 per hour; the authors consider it more indicative of typical exposure), both built from the single highest exhaled amount for each chemical and an assumed share of the inhaled amount (40% for local effects, 33% for systemic effects) appearing in the first exhalation. Modelled air concentrations (car / office): propylene glycol 9.5 / 2.16 mg/m3; nicotine 0.16 / 0.036 mg/m3; nitrosamines as NDMA equivalent 5.8 / 1.31 ng/m3; copper 219 / 50 ng/m3. Editors' calculation: the Table 5 values are reproduced from the Table 3 maxima and these settings.
Results › 3.7 Propylene Glycol; 3.9 and 3.10 Nicotine; 3.11 Nitrosamines; 3.12 Copper; Table 6; Conclusions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

The authors call the effects on bystanders relatively mild even in extreme scenarios, say the nitrosamine risk could be avoided if liquids had no detectable nitrosamines and that only a limited number of liquids on the market contain significant amounts (no citation in the passage), and describe this, to the best of their knowledge, as the first toxicological risk assessment of e-cigarette vapour to bystanders. The abstract states that vaping can clearly affect bystanders' health and names glycerol as an irritant, although glycerol was below the limit of quantification in all 17 volunteers. Funding as printed: Dutch Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport; the authors declare no conflict of interest.
Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusions › Regulatory Implications; Abstract; Funding; Conflicts of Interest

As described by the National Academies, in volunteers vaping in chambers and rooms: five people who also smoked, two 5-minute sessions of their own devices, one-hour air nicotine 3.32 (SD 2.49) µg/m3 against undetectable at baseline and PM2.5 152 (86.8) against 32.4 µg/m3 at baseline, no change in carbon monoxide (Czogała 2014); 37 volunteers over 4 hours with cigalike and tank devices, nicotine 0.38 to 2.83 µg/m3 with propylene glycol and glycerol up but several-fold below workplace limits, benzene, isoprene and toluene up (a 2017 chamber study); four volunteers, particles rising but lower than for tobacco smoke (Protano 2017); nine volunteers for 2 hours in a café-like room, PM2.5 197 against 6 µg/m3 in control periods, nicotine 2.2 against below 0.04 µg/m3, with aluminium and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons also higher than in control periods (Schober 2014).

As described by the National Academies, two modelling studies (Logue 2017, Rostami 2016); the passage gives results for Logue 2017 only. In a home scenario the contribution of second-hand vapour did not exceed California 8-hour reference exposure levels except with a high-emitting device (4.8 V; up to 12 µg/m3 formaldehyde and 2.6 µg/m3 acrolein); in a bar scenario, formaldehyde (mean 135 µg/m3) and acrolein (28 µg/m3) exceeded the acute 1-hour level for the highest-emitting device and voltage and exceeded 8-hour levels in several bars under less intense vaping. Health-loss estimates (disability-adjusted life years; also Logue 2017) for device and voltage combinations were lower than, but in some instances comparable to, those estimated for second-hand tobacco smoke. The committee identified no study of health effects or early biomarkers of disease from second-hand e-cigarette aerosol.

As described by the National Academies, the four studies the committee drew on for exposure among non-smokers to emissions from e-cigarettes compared with cigarettes (two measured people, two measured air or surfaces): 15 people who had never smoked, in three 30-minute sessions, blood-count indexes unchanged after passive e-cigarette exposure and the antioxidant markers unchanged after any condition, while passive cigarette smoke raised white-cell, lymphocyte and granulocyte counts for at least an hour (Flouris 2012); 54 non-smokers at home, airborne nicotine (geometric mean) 0.13 µg/m3 in homes with someone vaping against 0.74 in homes with someone smoking (5.7 times) and salivary cotinine (geometric mean) 0.19 against 0.38 ng/mL (Ballbè 2014); a chamber (air measurements only), one-hour airborne nicotine 3.32 against 31.60 µg/m3 and PM2.5 151.7 against 819.3 µg/m3 for e-cigarettes against cigarettes, which the committee gives as 10 and 7 times (editors' calculation from the raw means: 9.5 and 5.4 times) (Czogała 2014); nicotine on household surfaces (wipe samples) detected in half of 8 vaping homes against all 6 smoking homes, averaging 7.7 against 1,303 µg/m2 in the homes where it was found (Bush and Goniewicz 2015).

evidence_set: As described by the National Academies, four studies compared emissions from e-cigarettes and combustible cigarettes (three laboratory studies and one comparison based on published literature). Using published data and assuming 15 puffs equal one cigarette, selected toxic compounds in smoke were 9- to 450-fold higher than in aerosol (Goniewicz et al., 2014). Of 150 chemicals examined, about 100 were detected in smoke and 16 were generated by one e-cigarette, and toxicants were 82% to more than 99% lower per puff in the aerosol depending on the list and puffing method (Margham et al., 2016). Smoke held about 1,500 times more harmful and potentially harmful constituents than aerosol or room air (Tayyarah and Long, 2014). Of 11 metals with smoke data, the aerosol of one cartomizer was higher for four (aluminium, iron, nickel, sodium), within the smoke range for five and lower for two (Williams et al., 2013). The committee's synthesis: aerosol is substantially less complex than smoke and, except for nicotine, exposure to potentially toxic substances under typical conditions of use is significantly lower (substantial evidence, Conclusion 5-3). The studies are laboratory measurements, not measurements in people.
Chapter 18 › Evidence Review: Methods, 1st paragraph; Evidence Review: Results › Comparison of Toxic Levels in E-Cigarettes and Combustible Tobacco Cigarettes, 3rd to 6th paragraphs and Synthesis

As described by the National Academies, studies that followed people who switched from cigarettes to e-cigarettes lasted from 5 days to 8 months; examples: a 12-week trial of 420 people (urinary biomarkers of benzene, acrolein and a nitrosamine fell); a 5-day trial of 105 people (urinary biomarkers 29% to 95% lower in those who switched partly or completely; exhaled carbon monoxide down 88% to 89% in the groups that switched completely or stopped all nicotine); 20 people over 2 weeks (a nitrosamine breakdown product, NNAL, down 57% after 1 week and 64% after 2 weeks); and 40 people over 4 weeks (carbon monoxide down 80% in those who only vaped and 52% in those who also smoked). One cross-sectional study compared 181 people who had used these products for a long time, in five groups: nitrosamine and volatile organic compound breakdown products were lower in people who only vaped, or only used nicotine replacement, than in people who smoked, and similar in people who smoked only, vaped and smoked, or used nicotine replacement and smoked (Shahab et al., 2017). Synthesis: all studies showed significantly reduced biomarkers of exposure to potentially toxic chemicals in people who switched, and nicotine intake in people who had stopped smoking and were experienced at vaping was comparable to that from cigarettes. Conclusion 18-1: conclusive evidence that completely substituting e-cigarettes for cigarettes reduces exposure to numerous toxicants and carcinogens (the committee's judgment).

As described by the National Academies, the committee found 15 longitudinal observational and cross-over studies of health outcomes in people who switched from cigarettes to e-cigarettes (follow-up from single sessions to about two years; several retrospective record reviews). Examples: a one-year randomised trial of 300 people found no significant differences in lung-function indexes between groups defined by what people did after the trial began, except one flow measure (forced expiratory flow 25-75%) that rose in those who quit smoking, with cough, phlegm and breathlessness falling over follow-up (Cibella et al., 2016); in 15 people white blood cell counts rose after cigarettes but not after e-cigarettes in 30-minute sessions (Flouris et al., 2012); in a cross-over study of 20 adults who smoked and 20 who did not, acute use of either product changed markers of oxidative stress and blood-vessel function, with flow-mediated dilation and vitamin E effects not statistically different between the products and the e-cigarette showing a lesser effect on three other markers (Carnevale et al., 2016); and gingival inflammation increased in 20 people after 2 weeks of vaping instead of smoking (Wadia et al., 2016). A cross-sectional study, a design the Methods say was left out of the 15, compared nasal biopsies from 12 people who vaped, 14 who smoked and 13 who did neither: immune genes suppressed in people who smoked were also suppressed in people who vaped, with more gene changes and stronger suppression (Martin et al., 2016). In cell studies 21 of 27, and in animal studies 3 of 5, favoured e-cigarettes as less harmful than cigarettes and none found them more harmful than cigarettes. Synthesis: health effects of e-cigarettes are still not well understood but current evidence points to them being less harmful than cigarettes; all but one of the human studies showed significant short-term improvements in people who switched, though most studies were small; some studies found similar harm and none found e-cigarettes more harmful among people who switched to exclusive e-cigarette use; whether e-cigarettes reduce health risk still needs support from epidemiological studies and randomised trials. Conclusion 18-2: substantial evidence that completely switching from regular cigarette use to e-cigarettes results in reduced short-term adverse health outcomes in several organ systems (the committee's judgment).

The editorial states that in July 2013 a group of 12 experts rated the relative harm of 12 nicotine-containing products on 14 criteria for harm to self and others (reference 1, Nutt et al., 2014, not read), concluding that combustible cigarettes were the most harmful and e-cigarettes substantially less harmful, and that the result was repeated in the popular media as e-cigarettes being 95% less risky or 95% less harmful than combustible cigarettes. It adds that the authors of the 2013 work noted as a limitation the lack of hard evidence for the harms of most products on most of the criteria (quoted from page 224 of that paper); that Public Health England and the Royal College of Physicians endorsed and publicised the assertion; that senior Public Health England staff emphasised the evidence underlying the figure despite its being lacking; and that much was written questioning the figure's validity in 2014 to 2016 (no source cited for the last two). All of this is the authors' account: none of the originals was read.

The authors argue that products today differ from those of July 2013 to the extent that the 2013 estimate, even if valid then, can no longer apply: many devices reach a power output 10 to 20 times that of most over-the-counter 2013 models and so make more aerosol, exposing the person vaping to more nicotine and other toxicants and people nearby to more of any harmful aerosol constituents, and raising the chance of malfunction; there are thousands of flavours whose lung toxicity is unknown; and liquids with protonated nicotine (nicotine salt) are widely marketed and, relative to free-base nicotine, are less aversive to inhale, which the authors say allows higher nicotine concentrations and likely more dependence. No source is cited in the text for the statements on power, flavours or dependence; reference 4 (Jackler and Ramamurthi, 2019, not read) is cited for the marketing of protonated nicotine liquids and the 'nicotine arms race'; the online Appendix A, a nonexhaustive list of evidence of harm, was not read.

The authors argue that differences in toxicant content between aerosol and smoke, by themselves, cannot show lesser lethality, because toxicity depends on the extent and mode of use; that propylene glycol is toxic when injected over days and that aerosols containing it and glycerol cause inflammation in human lungs (no source cited); and that, because the toxicants sometimes differ, so might the diseases. They also state that there is little doubt that people who only vape are unlikely to die of lung cancer caused by tobacco-specific nitrosamines or polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, largely absent from the aerosol, and that what diseases they may die of, and whether use hastens death, will be part of the evidence needed for valid risk estimates. The editorial offers no estimate of the size of the difference.

The review states that e-cigarettes are relatively new, diverse and changing rapidly, that long-term evidence is unavailable and that the products studied do not necessarily reflect current options (limited information on newer nicotine salt products). It describes confounding between the effects of e-cigarette use and of smoking as a major problem that statistical adjustment is unlikely to fully overcome, particularly for the health conditions most affected by smoking, because older people who vape generally smoke regularly, are trying to quit or have quit, while younger people who vape often do not smoke regularly; it concludes that people who have never smoked are the most reliable group in which to quantify the effects of e-cigarettes and that people neither smoking nor using e-cigarettes should be the main comparison group. Statements that e-cigarettes are safer than smoking, and terms such as tobacco harm reduction, may be useful when discussing the minority of people who smoke who use e-cigarettes to quit completely but are not applicable to people who do not smoke; comparisons with the effects of smoking do not permit reliable ascertainment of the direct health impact of e-cigarettes.

The review rated the certainty of evidence very low for most clinical and subclinical outcomes. It notes that the tobacco and related industries can influence research, so its risk-of-bias assessment took account of competing interests such as financial support from tobacco or pharmaceutical industries; it writes that risks of bias were noted across health outcomes, but significant concerns in other domains meant they were unlikely to have large effects on its interpretation or the overall certainty of evidence. It states that it applies the precautionary principle (exposure to an agent with uncertain effects to be avoided), which it considers appropriate when serious adverse impacts are scientifically plausible, particularly those affecting future generations. Products not reported as nicotine or non-nicotine were assumed to be largely nicotine e-cigarettes (Box 3 note).

Meta-analyses of 25 longitudinal studies found strong evidence that young people who have never smoked and who use e-cigarettes are about three times as likely as those who do not to start smoking tobacco and to go on to smoke regularly (residual confounding cannot be excluded; the review deemed the link likely causal on Bradford-Hill criteria); limited evidence that people who had stopped smoking and use e-cigarettes are about twice as likely to resume smoking. The review names this, with poisoning, dependence (addiction) and toxicity from inhalation, among the risks that disproportionately affect people who do not smoke and young people. This concerns the harm of starting to smoke, a different comparison from vaping against smoking, and the UK review left it out of its scope.
